name: Body makeup / leg makeup

lead: Body makeup, often sold as leg makeup or bronzer, gives you an even, tanned-looking finish on the day. It covers blemishes and marks and adds colour in a single application, so skin looks smoother in photos and at events.

It works by depositing a temporary tint on the surface of the skin, which is why the result shows immediately and comes off with soap and water. It is used as a quick alternative or add-on to self-tanner. No clinical studies have examined it; the effect is visible straight away.

paras: People apply it to legs, arms or shoulders shortly before a photo, event or night out, in forms such as powders, sprays, mousses, gels and lotions. It is often used on top of a self-tan for extra depth, and it is removed the same day with soap and water.

Reported drawbacks are rub-off onto clothing, and orange or uneven results if applied unevenly. Some formulations contain allergens such as fragrances or benzyl alcohol, which matters for anyone with sensitive skin.

angle.text: Body and leg makeup tints the skin so tone looks even, marks are covered and colour is added for a photo or event. The result is visible immediately and washes off with soap and water, so it works as a same-day look.

lead: Body makeup, often sold as leg makeup, is a cosmetic applied to the skin below the face to even out tone, cover marks and add colour, usually for a photo, stage, event or sun-free tan. Wikipedia describes foundation applied to the body as body makeup, with sheer to full coverage depending on the formula [1]. For appearance, it can make legs and arms look more uniform and tanned, and full-coverage products are used to cover birthmarks, vitiligo, hyperpigmentation and scars [1].

Temporary bronzers belong to the same family. Wikipedia lists them as powders, sprays, mousses, gels and lotions that tint the surface of the skin and wash off with soap and water, mostly for one-day tans or alongside a DHA self-tanner [2]. Some lotions contain a gradual tanning agent so colour builds with repeated use [2].

In looksmaxxing forums, bronzer and contour are discussed mostly for the face, with posters saying they brighten dull skin tone and sharpen features [3][4]. Wikipedia's article on male cosmetics notes that men use cosmetics to cover skin flaws, for stage and film work and to slow aging, that stigma in the US has weakened, and that male beauty influencers on YouTube and other platforms have grown in number [5]. Reported drawbacks of tinted body products are rub-off onto clothes and an orange or blotchy look if applied unevenly [2]. No published trials have tested body makeup for appearance outcomes.

paras: Temporary bronzing and tinting products colour only the surface of the skin and do not involve the chemical reaction that DHA self-tanners use; like make-up, they tint skin only until they are washed off [2]. Bronzers come as powders, sprays, mousses, gels, lotions and moisturisers, and common ingredients include walnut oil extract, jojoba extract and caramel colour [2]. Wikipedia notes that the term bronzer is not legally defined and that the FDA regulates DHA, the colourless colour additive used in self-tanners [2].

Body makeup proper is foundation applied below the face, sometimes called body painting [1]. Foundation formulas include oil or emollient-based (the oldest type, thick and opaque), alcohol-based, powder-based (starting with Max Factor's Pan-Cake, with talc as the main ingredient), mineral, water-based (which emerged after World War II once emulsifiers could stabilise water-and-oil blends, with transfer-resistant polymer-based versions first appearing in 1993) and silicone-based types, with coverage from sheer to full [1].

Wikipedia lists common application tools: fingers, whose warmth helps blend sheer layers but which can streak at full coverage; sponges for sheer to medium coverage; brushes, with synthetic bristles for liquids and natural bristles for powders; and airbrushes, which spray foundation as fine droplets for an even finish and are also common in special-effects work [1]. Airbrush-style spray products sold for legs follow this approach. Tinted products can leave light rub-off where fabric meets skin, though dark clothing hides it, and misapplied product can look orange or blotchy [2].

Medium coverage can hide freckles, discolouration and pimple marks, while full coverage is used for birthmarks, vitiligo, hyperpigmentation and scars [1]. Bronzers are used for a one-day tan or to complement a self-tan [2]. A poster on looksmax.org argued that bronzer with BB cream brightened dull skin tone and made weak skin quality less noticeable [3], and another thread described bronzer and contouring with fake tan as a way to change the look of the face considerably [4]. For legs and arms, people use the same products to even out colour between body and a tanned or made-up face for photos, events or the stage.

Cosmetic camouflage is the use of makeup creams or powders to hide colour or contour irregularities of the face or body; Wikipedia says plastic surgeons first developed such creams during World War II to cover severe burns on fighter pilots. [6] The article describes green concealer used sparingly over red areas, for example after eyelid surgery or on port-wine stains. [6] Full-coverage body foundation sits in the same family and is used for birthmarks, vitiligo, hyperpigmentation and scars. [1]

For vitiligo, Wikipedia says mild cases can be hidden with makeup or other cosmetic camouflage products, and that for pale-skinned people avoiding tanning of unaffected skin can make patches less noticeable. It adds that the altered appearance can affect emotional wellbeing and employment, and that support groups may help with social coping. [7] Camouflage products are also used to cover scars and tattoos.

Makeup applied to the body appears in performance and competition settings. Wikipedia notes that most bodybuilders tan and shave their bodies before competition, and the practice of colouring and evening the skin tone under stage lighting is part of presentation for physique shows, pageants and modelling shoots. [8] Judging criteria in bodybuilding are listed as conditioning, muscularity, posing, size, stage presentation and symmetry. [8]

Body painting is a related but separate practice in which artwork is painted directly onto the skin; modern water-based face and body paints are described as non-toxic, usually non-allergenic and easy to wash off, and applied by hand, brush, sponge or airbrush. [9] A 2017 paper in the Journal of Perioperative Practice treats body makeup alongside dress codes and artificial gadgets as ways people enhance personal appearance, in the context of how fashion trends affect anaesthetic practice. [10]

sections.h: Use in looksmaxxing and male grooming
paras: On looksmax.org, bronzer and contour appear under the heading of 'softmax' tools: low-risk, reversible cosmetic changes to skin tone and facial definition. One poster argued that bronzer with BB cream makes dull skin look brighter and weak skin quality less noticeable. [3] Another described bronzer, contour and fake tan together as close to cosmetic surgery without the surgery, adding that male actors and celebrities use them and that the result depends on doing it well and on the underlying features. [4] Replies in the second thread debated whether male makeup tutorials suit the community's aesthetic, with some members saying they wanted to learn more. [4]

Wikipedia traces male cosmetics use to ancient Egypt, Rome and Elizabethan England, notes that men's beauty products were largely absent from the market until the late 1990s, and says men aged 18 to 34 are the most likely users. [5] Packaging for men's lines tends toward muted colours such as blue, green, grey and black. [5]

In the US the FDA does not require pre-market approval for cosmetics or their ingredients, except colour additives, and manufacturers are responsible for safety; the EU regulates cosmetics under Regulation EC 1223/2009 with a responsible person and product information file for each product. [11] Wikipedia notes that bronzer is not a legally defined category and that the FDA regulates DHA, the colourless additive in self-tanners. [2] Ingredients are listed in descending order by weight, with fragrance allowed as a collective term in the US. [11]

Concerns described in references include fragrance allergens as a main source of contact allergy, PFAS, formaldehyde releasers and, historically, lead-based products. [11] Body-paint guidance advises stopping use if skin shows signs of allergy, avoiding application to damaged or inflamed skin, using only products formulated for the body, and noting that some dyes are not approved for use near the eyes or lips. [9]

Foundation has a long history. Ancient Egyptians used foundation, and around 200 BC Greek women used white lead powder and chalk to lighten the skin; lead-based paints and ceruse remained in use for centuries, and men also lightened their skin, with lead-based makeup fashionable at the court of Louis XV in 18th-century France [1]. The German theatre figure Carl Baudin invented greasepaint, Max Factor created Flexible Greasepaint suited to film lighting in 1914, and Factor patented Pan-Cake in 1937 as the first commercially available foundation, which by 1940 an estimated one in three North American women owned [1].

Sunless tanning developed in parallel. Eva Wittgenstein discovered the skin-staining effect of DHA at Cincinnati Children's Hospital in the 1950s, Man-Tan became the first commercial DHA self-tanner in 1959 and Coppertone's QT followed in 1960; both gave orange-toned results, and reformulated products and, from the late 1990s, automated spray-tan booths widened the market [2]. Wash-off bronzers remained a separate, temporary category.

Listed drawbacks include limited sweat or water resistance in some formulas, transfer onto clothing and uneven results [2]. Some formulations contain possible allergens such as benzyl alcohol, tocopherol and fragrances [2]. A 2021 study cited by Wikipedia tested 231 makeup and personal-care products and found organic fluorine, an indicator of PFAS, in more than half, including 63 percent of foundations; manufacturers often do not label PFAS content [1]. Wikipedia calls bronzers much safer than tanning beds [2].
